lessons.title: Computers and data: what it is and how big it is
lessons.summary: A computer takes data in, processes it, stores it and gives it out — and it measures everything in bytes.
objectives: Explain input, process, output and storage with real examples
Say what a bit and a byte are
Read KB, MB, GB and TB, and check free space on a device
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Name the input, process, output and storage when you send a voice note
- Order six files from smallest to largest by their size
- Find how much free storage your phone or the lab computer has

## Understand it

Everything a computer handles is **data**: the letters you type, a photo, a song, your marks, a location.

Every device does four things with it:

1. **Input** — data comes in (keyboard, touchscreen, camera, microphone).
2. **Process** — the processor works on it (resizes the photo, adds the numbers).
3. **Output** — it comes back out (screen, speaker, printer).
4. **Storage** — it is kept for later (phone storage, a hard drive, a flash drive, the cloud).

Inside, all of it is stored as **bits** — 0s and 1s. Eight bits make a **byte**, about one letter. Bigger amounts go up in steps of about a thousand: **KB** (kilobyte), **MB** (megabyte), **GB** (gigabyte), **TB** (terabyte). A text message is a few KB; a phone photo 2–5 MB; an hour of video around 1 GB.

Why it matters: when a phone says "storage full", when a file is "too large to attach", or when a data bundle runs out, it is these units you are reading.

![How big is data?](media:core/storage-units.svg)

## Key words

- **Data:** facts, words, sounds or pictures a computer can store and process
- **Bit:** a single 0 or 1
- **Byte:** 8 bits — about one character
- **Storage:** where data is kept when the device is off

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Computer Basics](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/computerbasics/) — Free, illustrated, no account: do the lesson named in class, then its quiz.

## Practise at home

- Check the storage on a phone at home: what uses the most?
- Work out how many 3 MB photos fit in 1 GB of free space

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Use the picture: each step to the right is about 1,000 of the one before.
- **If you already can:** Find out why a "64 GB" phone shows less than 64 GB free, and explain it in two sentences.

## Assessed this week

- Which is the LARGEST amount of data?
- When you take a photo and post it, name the input, process, output and storage.
- Show your instructor how much free storage a device has, and what is using the most space.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Files, folders and good names
lessons.summary: A file is one piece of saved work; folders keep them organised; a good name finds it again in six months.
objectives: Create, rename, move and delete files and folders
Read a file's extension and path
Name files so they sort and can be found
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Make a folder called Data Appreciation with three sub-folders
- Save, rename and move a file into it
- Find a file using search, then by following its path

## Understand it

A **file** is one saved thing — a document, a photo, a spreadsheet. A **folder** holds files and other folders, like drawers in a cabinet. The route from the top to a file is its **path**: `Documents › Club › Data Appreciation › lunch-survey.xlsx`.

The last part of a file name after the dot is the **extension**. It tells you the file type and which app opens it: `.docx` a document, `.xlsx` a spreadsheet, `.jpg` a photo, `.pdf` a finished page.

Good names save hours:

- **Start with the date, year first** — `2026-03-14_` — so files sort in order.
- **Say what it is** and **which version**: `lunch-survey_v2`.
- Never `final`, `final2`, `finalFINAL`.

The everyday actions: **New folder**, **Rename**, **Move** (drag, or cut and paste), **Copy**, **Delete** (it goes to the Recycle Bin or Trash first, so it can be restored).

![A file manager: the path at the top, files named date-first, and the type from the extension](media:core/shots/file-manager.png)

![Files, folders and names](media:core/file-tree.svg)

## Key words

- **File:** one saved piece of work
- **Folder:** a container for files and other folders
- **Extension:** the letters after the dot that give the file type
- **Path:** a file's address, folder by folder

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Operating systems and files](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/computerbasics/understanding-operating-systems/1/) — How a computer organises files; read it with your own file manager open.
- [GCFGlobal — Computer Basics](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/computerbasics/) — Free, illustrated, no account: do the lesson named in class, then its quiz.

## Practise at home

- Tidy the downloads folder on a home device (ask first)
- Rename three files using the date-first pattern

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Follow the picture: make the folders first, then save into them.
- **If you already can:** Find where a deleted file goes on your device and restore one.

## Assessed this week

- Put the steps for saving a new file into a new folder in order.
- A file is called `2026-03-14_report_v3.pdf`. What does `.pdf` tell you?
- Show your Data Appreciation folder with three sub-folders and two files named date-first.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Saving, storage and backups
lessons.summary: Know where your work is saved — on the device, a flash drive or the cloud — and keep a backup before you need it.
objectives: Tell device storage, removable storage and cloud storage apart
Use Save and Save As correctly
Make a backup plan with the 3-2-1 rule
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Save a file twice: once with Save, once with Save As to a new name
- Copy it to a flash drive or cloud drive
- Write your own 3-2-1 backup plan

## Understand it

Where can a file live?

- **On the device** — the phone or laptop itself. Fast, but lost with the device.
- **Removable storage** — a flash drive (USB) or memory card. Carry it anywhere; easy to lose.
- **The cloud** — your files kept on a company's computers over the internet (Google Drive, OneDrive, iCloud). Reached from any device, but needs data and a strong password.

**Save** keeps changes in the same file. **Save As** makes a new copy with a new name or place — use it before big changes, so the old version survives.

The **3-2-1 rule**: keep **3** copies of anything important, on **2** different kinds of storage, with **1** somewhere else (the cloud, or away from home). Phones are lost, stolen and dropped; a project that exists in one place is a project you can lose the day before it is due.

![The 3-2-1 backup rule](media:core/backup-321.svg)

## Key words

- **Cloud storage:** files kept on servers you reach over the internet
- **Save As:** save a copy with a new name or place
- **Backup:** an extra copy kept in case the original is lost
- **Sync:** keeping the same files up to date on several devices

## Read and watch

- [NCSC — Back up your data](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/always-back-up-your-most-important-data) — Official, plain-English steps: follow them on one of your own devices.
- [GCFGlobal — Computer Basics](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/computerbasics/) — Free, illustrated, no account: do the lesson named in class, then its quiz.

## Practise at home

- Find out where the photos on a home phone are backed up, if anywhere
- Write the 3-2-1 plan for your schoolwork

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Fill the three boxes of the picture with YOUR devices.
- **If you already can:** Find out what happens to a cloud file you delete: is there a bin, and for how long?

## Assessed this week

- Your only copy of a project is on your phone. Which change makes it safest?
- Follow the NCSC backup steps on one of your devices (with a parent if it is theirs). Paste a screenshot of the backup turned on, and say what it backs up.
- Write your own 3-2-1 backup plan: the three copies, the two kinds of storage, and the one kept elsewhere.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: The keyboard, shortcuts and entering data accurately
lessons.summary: Fast is good; accurate is essential. Shortcuts save time, and consistent data entry saves everyone after you.
objectives: Use ten everyday keyboard shortcuts
Type with accuracy before speed
Enter data consistently: dates, names, numbers
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Practise the ten shortcuts on a document
- Do a two-minute typing test and record accuracy
- Find and fix five inconsistent entries in a list

## Understand it

Ten shortcuts every user should know (on a Mac, Cmd instead of Ctrl):

- **Ctrl+C** copy · **Ctrl+X** cut · **Ctrl+V** paste
- **Ctrl+Z** undo · **Ctrl+Y** redo
- **Ctrl+S** save · **Ctrl+F** find
- **Ctrl+A** select all · **Ctrl+P** print · **Alt+Tab** switch window

Typing: eyes on the screen, fingers home on **ASDF JKL;**, and **accuracy first** — fixing errors costs more than typing slowly.

**Entering data** is where most mistakes start. A list where one person wrote `14/3/26`, another `March 14` and a third `14-03-2026` cannot be sorted. Agree a format before you start and keep it: one date format, the same spelling every time (`Egbeda`, never `egbeda` or `Egbedda`), numbers with no units typed in (`900`, with `₦` in the heading). Then check: read it back, or have a partner read it.

![Ten everyday shortcuts](media:core/shortcuts.svg)

## Key words

- **Shortcut:** a key combination that does a command
- **Accuracy:** the share of what you typed that was right
- **Consistent:** always done the same way

## Read and watch

- [Monkeytype](https://monkeytype.com/) — Free typing practice in a browser, no account needed: aim for accuracy first, speed second.
- [GCFGlobal — Computer Basics](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/computerbasics/) — Free, illustrated, no account: do the lesson named in class, then its quiz.

## Practise at home

- Do three typing tests at home and record accuracy each time
- Use five shortcuts while doing homework

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Learn three shortcuts this week — copy, paste, undo — and add more next week.
- **If you already can:** Find the shortcut for a new tab, closing a window and taking a screenshot on your device.

## Assessed this week

- Take a two-minute typing test on Monkeytype and paste a screenshot of your result. Say your accuracy and one thing you will change.
- A class list has dates written as 14/3/26, March 14 and 14-03-2026. What is the main problem?
- Fix the inconsistent list your instructor gives you: one date format, one spelling per place, no units in the numbers.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets I: cells, rows, columns and formatting
lessons.summary: A spreadsheet is a grid for data: learn its parts, enter data cleanly and make it readable.
objectives: Name a cell by its column and row
Enter text, numbers and dates and format them
Make a table readable: headers, widths, number formats
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Open a new spreadsheet in Google Sheets or LibreOffice Calc
- Build a shopping budget table with five items
- Format the headers, the ₦ column and the widths

## Understand it

A spreadsheet is a grid.

- **Columns** are lettered A, B, C… and run down.
- **Rows** are numbered 1, 2, 3… and run across.
- A **cell** is where they meet, named column-then-row: **B6**.
- The **formula bar** shows what is really in the selected cell.

Entering data: click a cell, type, press **Enter** (down) or **Tab** (right). One value per cell. Put headings in row 1.

Formatting makes it readable without changing the data:

- **Bold** the header row and **freeze** it (View → Freeze → 1 row).
- Widen columns (double-click the edge between column letters).
- Number formats: currency for money, a date format for dates, 0 or 2 decimal places as needed.
- Align numbers right, text left.

A number formatted as currency is still a number — you can add it up. A number typed as `₦900` text cannot be added: format, don't type the symbol.

![The parts of a spreadsheet](media:core/spreadsheet-anatomy.svg)

## Key words

- **Cell:** one box of the grid, named like B6
- **Column / row:** a vertical line of cells (letter) / a horizontal one (number)
- **Format:** how a value looks, without changing the value

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Google Sheets](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/googlespreadsheets/) — Step-by-step spreadsheet lessons with practice files; work through the one named in class.
- [LibreOffice Calc Help](https://help.libreoffice.org/latest/en-US/text/scalc/main0000.html) — The free, offline spreadsheet: every step today works in it too.

## Practise at home

- Build a table of your week's spending or screen time
- Format it so a parent can read it at a glance

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Copy the picture's table exactly first, then change the items.
- **If you already can:** Add conditional formatting: colour any amount over ₦2,000.

## Assessed this week

- The cell in column C, row 4 is called…
- Show your formatted budget table: a bold frozen header, readable widths, and the money in currency format.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Spreadsheets II: formulas that do the work
lessons.summary: Formulas calculate for you, and recalculate when the data changes: SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT — and fill down.
objectives: Write formulas with SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX and COUNT
Fill a formula across or down
Explain relative and absolute references
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Add a total row to your budget with SUM
- Fill it across three days
- Work out a 7.5% charge using an absolute reference

## Understand it

A **formula** starts with **=**. A **function** is a named calculation; a **range** is the cells it works on.

- `=SUM(B2:B5)` adds B2 to B5.
- `=AVERAGE(B2:B5)` · `=MIN(…)` · `=MAX(…)` · `=COUNT(…)` counts numbers.
- `=B2*C2` multiplies two cells; `+ - * /` all work.

Change a number and every formula that uses it updates. That is the whole point: never type a total you could calculate.

**Fill**: drag the small square at the corner of a cell. The references move with it — `=SUM(B2:B5)` becomes `=SUM(C2:C5)` one column right. That is a **relative** reference.

Sometimes one cell must NOT move — a tax rate in E1. Write it `$E$1`: an **absolute** reference. `=B2*$E$1` filled down always uses E1.

If you ask an AI chatbot to write a formula, test it on numbers you can check by hand before you trust it — it is often confidently wrong about ranges.

![Worked example: SUM in B6, filled right to C6 and D6](media:core/shots/sheets-sum.png)

![Reading a formula](media:core/formula.svg)

## Key words

- **Formula:** a calculation that starts with =
- **Function:** a named calculation such as SUM
- **Range:** a block of cells, like B2:B5
- **Absolute reference:** a reference with $ that does not move when filled

## Read and watch

- [Google Sheets function list](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Look up any formula used today — AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE, COUNTIF.
- [GCFGlobal — Google Sheets](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/googlespreadsheets/) — Step-by-step spreadsheet lessons with practice files; work through the one named in class.

## Practise at home

- Add totals and an average to the table you made last week
- Change one number and watch the totals update

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Type the formula from the picture exactly, then change only the range.
- **If you already can:** Use COUNTIF to count how many days spending went over ₦2,000.

## Assessed this week

- Write a formula to find the average of the values in D2 to D10.
- C6 holds =SUM(C2:C5). You fill it one column right into D6. What does D6 hold?
- Complete the GCFGlobal Google Sheets lesson on formulas and functions and its practice; paste proof and one formula you wrote yourself.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Sort, filter, find and tidy data
lessons.summary: Answer questions from a long list in seconds — if the table is tidy and you sort the whole thing.
objectives: Sort a whole table by one column
Filter to show only some rows
Use Find and Replace, and keep data tidy
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Sort the survey table by age, then by name
- Filter to show only one answer
- Use Find and Replace to fix a misspelling everywhere

## Understand it

A table is **tidy** when it has one row per thing, one column per question, one value per cell, and a header row. Then the spreadsheet can answer questions for you.

- **Sort**: select the WHOLE table, then **Data → Sort range**, with "has header row" ticked. Never sort a single column — it scrambles every row.
- **Filter**: **Data → Create a filter**, then pick values in a column. Other rows are **hidden, not deleted** — turn the filter off and they come back.
- **Find** (Ctrl+F) locates a word; **Find and Replace** (Ctrl+H) fixes it everywhere at once. Check the count before you press Replace all.

![Filter on: only Jollof shows; the row numbers jump because the other rows are hidden](media:core/shots/sheets-sort-filter.png)

![A tidy table](media:core/tidy-data.svg)

## Key words

- **Sort:** put rows in order by a column
- **Filter:** show only some rows, without deleting the rest
- **Tidy data:** one row per thing, one column per question

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Google Sheets](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/googlespreadsheets/) — Step-by-step spreadsheet lessons with practice files; work through the one named in class.
- [Google Sheets function list](https://support.google.com/docs/table/25273) — Look up any formula used today — AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MODE, COUNTIF.

## Practise at home

- Sort a list of family birthdays by month
- Filter it to show this term's

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Always click inside the table first, then use Data → Sort range.
- **If you already can:** Sort by two columns: first by centre, then by name within each centre.

## Assessed this week

- Why should you never sort only ONE column of a table?
- Show the survey table sorted by one column, filtered to one answer, and one spelling fixed with Find and Replace.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Work out mean, median and mode for pocket money
- Choose the chart for three questions
- Make a bar chart with a title, labels and source

## Understand it

Three "averages":

- **Mean** = add them up, divide by how many: `=AVERAGE()`. One huge value drags it.
- **Median** = the middle value when sorted: `=MEDIAN()`. Not moved by one odd value.
- **Mode** = the most common: `=MODE()`.

When one value is far from the rest (an **outlier**), the median describes a typical person better.

Charts answer questions: **bar** to compare groups, **line** for change over time, **pie** only for a few parts of one whole, **scatter** for whether two things go together. In Sheets: select the table → **Insert → Chart** → pick the type. A chart someone else can read has a **title that says what it shows**, **labelled axes**, the **source** and the **date**, and bar charts start at **zero**.

![Worked example: a labelled bar chart, axis from 0](media:core/shots/sheets-chart.png)

![An outlier and three averages](media:core/averages.svg)

![Choose the chart by the question](media:core/chart-chooser.svg)

## Key words

- **Mean / median / mode:** the arithmetic average / the middle / the most common
- **Outlier:** a value far from the rest
- **Axis:** the scale along the side or bottom of a chart

## Read and watch

- [Khan Academy — Statistics and probability](https://www.khanacademy.org/math/statistics-probability) — Short videos and practice that check themselves; do the set named in the lesson.
- [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/) — Real charts about the whole world, each with its source — read them like a detective.

## Practise at home

- Find mean and median of your screen time for a week; say which is fairer
- Find a chart in the news and say if it is labelled properly

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Sort the numbers first: the median and mode jump out.
- **If you already can:** Find a bar chart whose axis does not start at zero and redraw it honestly.

## Assessed this week

- Pocket money (₦): 200, 300, 300, 300, 400, 500, 600, 3000. Which best describes a typical child?

lessons.summary: Search well, then check before you believe or share: who made it, when, and what do other trusted sources say?
objectives: Use search operators to find better results

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Search the same question three ways and compare
- Check one viral claim with SIFT
- Find the original source of a statistic

## Understand it

Better searching:

- **"quotes"** find an exact phrase: `"Lagos population"`.
- **site:** searches one site: `site:nigerianstat.gov.ng inflation`.
- **-word** removes results: `jaguar -car`.
- Add the year for recent facts: `2026`.

Before you believe or share, use **SIFT**:

1. **Stop** — do you know this site or person?
2. **Investigate the source** — who made it, when, why?
3. **Find better coverage** — what do trusted sources say?
4. **Trace** claims back to the original data or quote.

A screenshot is not a source. A number with no source, date or link is a claim, not a fact.

AI chatbots answer fluently and are sometimes wrong, with invented sources. Use an answer as a list of things to check, and check them.

![SIFT: four moves before you share](media:core/sift.svg)

## Key words

- **Search operator:** a symbol or word that narrows a search
- **Source:** who or where information comes from
- **Misinformation:** false information, shared by mistake or on purpose

## Read and watch

- [SIFT — the four moves](https://hapgood.us/2019/06/19/sift-the-four-moves/) — A fact-checker's four quick moves for anything you read online.
- [Our World in Data](https://ourworldindata.org/) — Real charts about the whole world, each with its source — read them like a detective.

## Practise at home

- Check one message forwarded in a family group with SIFT
- Explain your verdict to someone at home

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Do SIFT as a checklist on paper: tick each move.
- **If you already can:** Find a statistic quoted in the news and trace it to the original table.

## Assessed this week

- A post says "80% of students fail maths" with no link. What is the best first step?

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

lessons.title: Staying safe: passwords, scams and personal data
lessons.summary: Protect your accounts and other people's data: strong passwords, 2-step verification, spotting scams, and the law.
objectives: Make a strong passphrase and turn on 2-step verification
Spot a phishing message
Say what personal data is and what Nigeria's data law protects
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Turn a weak password into a strong passphrase
- Find the five warning signs in a scam message
- Turn on 2-step verification on one account (with a parent)

## Understand it

**Passwords**: long beats clever. Three or four random words — `plum-river-kettle-sunday` — are strong and memorable. Use a **different** one for every account, especially email (it can reset all the others). A password manager remembers them.

**2-step verification (2FA)**: a code from your phone as well as the password. A stolen password alone then opens nothing.

**Phishing** messages try to make you click, pay or log in. Warning signs: urgency ("within 24 hours"), a prize you did not enter, a sender address that is nearly right, a link that goes somewhere odd, a request for a code or password. No real bank or school asks for your password or OTP.

**Updates** fix security holes: install them.

**Personal data** — names, phone numbers, photos, addresses, marks — belongs to the person it describes. The **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** says: ask first, collect only what you need, keep it safe, share it with nobody who should not have it.

![Strong passwords and 2FA](media:core/passwords.svg)

## Key words

- **Passphrase:** a password made of several random words
- **2-step verification:** a second check, usually a code on your phone
- **Phishing:** a message pretending to be someone trusted to steal details

## Read and watch

- [NCSC — Strong, separate passwords](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/collection/top-tips-for-staying-secure-online/use-a-strong-and-separate-password-for-email) — Why three random words beat a clever password, and how to start.
- [NCSC — Turn on 2-step verification](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/setting-two-step-verification-2sv) — How to switch on the second lock for your email and other accounts.
- [NCSC — Spotting a suspicious message](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/guidance/suspicious-email-actions) — What to do when a message asks you to click, pay or log in.
- [Nigeria Data Protection Commission](https://ndpc.gov.ng/) — Who protects personal data in Nigeria, and what the law (NDPA 2023) promises you.

## Practise at home

- With a parent, check which accounts at home have 2-step verification
- Show someone at home the five phishing signs

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Use the picture: make your passphrase from four things you can see in the room.
- **If you already can:** Find out what a data breach is and check how to tell if your email was in one.

## Assessed this week

- A message says your bank account will close today unless you send the code you just received. What should you do?
- Show 2-step verification turned on for one account (yours or, with permission, a family one), and explain what it protects against.
- Which piece of personal data about you would you least want shared, and why? (Private to your instructor.)

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.

objectives: Choose a file type for the job (PDF, DOCX, XLSX, CSV, JPG, PNG)

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Export your budget as a PDF and as a CSV
- Share your sheet with a partner as a commenter
- Restore an earlier version from version history

## Understand it

**Pick the file type for the job.** Still being edited? Send the editable file (`.docx`, `.xlsx`). Finished and must look the same everywhere? **PDF**. Data for another app? **CSV**. Photos **JPG**; screenshots and logos **PNG**.

**Attachment or link?** An attachment is a copy — edits do not travel back. A shared link points to ONE file everybody works on.

**Access**: give the least that does the job.

- **Viewer** reads · **Commenter** suggests · **Editor** changes.
- **Restricted** (only people you add) is the safe default; "anyone with the link" travels further than you think — never for personal data.

**Working together**: use **comments** instead of typing into someone's work, and **version history** (File → Version history) to see who changed what and to restore an older version.

![A share dialog: each person given only the access they need, general access Restricted](media:core/shots/share-dialog.png)

![File types and what they are for](media:core/file-formats.svg)

![Sharing permissions](media:core/sharing.svg)

## Key words

- **PDF:** a finished page that looks the same everywhere
- **CSV:** plain table data any app can read
- **Permission:** what someone is allowed to do with a shared file
- **Version history:** the record of earlier versions of a file

## Read and watch

The panel will ask about YOUR choices: why that format, why that chart, how it is backed up. That is how they know the work is yours.

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Collect five printed things (a flyer, a programme, a receipt, a certificate, a menu)
- Say who each is for and what it must do
- Open Canva and one other free tool

## Understand it

**Desktop publishing (DTP)** is arranging text and pictures on a page so people can read and use it: flyers, posters, newsletters, certificates, brochures, programmes, menus.

Good design is not decoration. A flyer must be read in three seconds from across the road; a programme must be found in the dark; a certificate must look official.

The tools (all free):

- **Canva** — browser and phone, templates, easy sharing.
- **Google Docs / Slides** — quick documents and single pages.
- **LibreOffice Draw/Writer** — offline, on any computer.
- **Scribus** — professional page layout for print, free.

(Microsoft Publisher's support ends in October 2026, so it is not taught here.)

## Key words

- **Desktop publishing:** designing pages of text and pictures
- **Layout:** where things sit on the page
- **Template:** a starting design you adapt

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Beginning Graphic Design](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/beginning-graphic-design/) — Free, short, illustrated lessons on layout, type and colour; no account needed.
- [Scribus](https://www.scribus.net/) — Free, professional desktop publishing for Windows, Mac and Linux — what the print trade uses for free.
- [LibreOffice Help](https://help.libreoffice.org/) — Free office suite; Draw and Writer can lay out a flyer or newsletter.

## Practise at home

## Understand it

**A-sizes** halve each time: A3 folded in half is A4; A4 folded is A5. A4 (210 × 297 mm) is the standard Nigerian document page; A5 is a handy flyer; A3 a small poster.

**Orientation**: portrait (tall) or landscape (wide). Choose by the content — a list is tall, a timeline is wide.

**Margins** are the empty border. They make a page look calm, stop text being cut off, and leave room for fingers. Keep at least 10–15 mm on a printed page. In Google Docs: **File → Page setup**; in Canva: choose a custom size in mm.

Decide the size FIRST: changing it later moves everything.

- **A4:** 210 × 297 mm, the standard document page
- **Portrait / landscape:** tall / wide orientation
- **Margin:** the empty border around the page

objectives: Tell serif from sans-serif fonts

Use at most two fonts on a page
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Compare three fonts on the same paragraph
- Find the size where your partner reads it easily at arm's length
- Set line spacing and line length

## Understand it

- **Serif** fonts have small strokes at the ends of letters (Georgia, Times); **sans-serif** fonts do not (Arial, Inter). Both are readable; pick one for body text and keep it.
- **Size**: body text for print is usually 10–12 pt; for screens 16 px. Headings are bigger.
- **Line length**: 45–75 characters per line is comfortable. Longer lines tire the eye.
- **Line spacing**: about 1.2–1.5 times the font size.
- **Two fonts at most**: one for headings, one for body. Never decorative fonts for body text.

CAPITALS are hard to read in long stretches, and underline looks like a link. Use **bold** for emphasis.

## Key words

- **Font:** a style of lettering
- **Serif:** small strokes at the ends of letters
- **Sans-serif:** without those strokes
- **Leading:** the space between lines

## Read and watch

- [Google Fonts Knowledge](https://fonts.google.com/knowledge) — Short, clear lessons on type: read the one named in the lesson.

lessons.title: Type II: hierarchy — what to read first
lessons.summary: Size, weight and colour tell the reader what matters most. A clear hierarchy gets the message across in seconds.
objectives: Build a five-level hierarchy
Use size, weight and colour — not many fonts

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Rank the information on a flyer by importance
- Give each level its own size and weight
- Test it: what does a partner remember after three seconds?

## Understand it

**Hierarchy** is the order the eye reads in. Most pages need about five levels:

1. **Headline** — biggest, boldest: what it is.
2. **Subheading** — supports the headline.
3. **Key facts** — when, where, how much (often in a coloured block).
4. **Body** — the details, at a comfortable size.
5. **Caption / small print** — smallest.

Make each level clearly different: **size** (headline 3× body), **weight** (bold vs regular), **colour** (one accent), and **space** around it. If everything is big and bold, nothing stands out.

The test: show it to someone for three seconds. They should remember the headline and the key facts.

![Five levels of text](media:core/type-hierarchy.svg)

## Key words

- **Hierarchy:** the order of importance shown by size, weight and colour
- **Weight:** how thick the letters are: regular, bold
- **Accent colour:** one colour used to point at what matters

## Read and watch

- Do the three-second test on a family member

objectives: Use a column grid to place things

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Draw a 3-column grid on an A4 page
- Place a headline, photo and two stories on it
- Critique a classmate's page with the four principles

## Understand it

A **grid** divides the page into columns with gaps (**gutters**). Everything snaps to the columns, so the page looks orderly even with many parts. A headline might span three columns, a photo two, a sidebar one.

Four principles to check every page:

- **Contrast** — make different things look very different (headline vs body).
- **Repetition** — repeat fonts, colours and shapes so the page feels like one thing.
- **Alignment** — every item lines up with something; nothing is placed "by eye".
- **Proximity** — put related things close together and unrelated things apart.

White space is not wasted space: it gives the eye somewhere to rest.

![A three-column grid](media:core/grid.svg)

## Key words

- **Grid:** columns that guide where things go
- **Gutter:** the gap between columns
- **White space:** empty space that lets a design breathe

lessons.title: Colour: schemes, contrast, and screen vs print
lessons.summary: Use few colours, make text readable, and remember that screens and printers make colour differently.
objectives: Build a colour scheme from the colour wheel
Check text contrast (aim for 4.5:1)
Explain RGB versus CMYK
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pick a scheme on the colour wheel
- Test your text colours in a contrast checker
- Compare a bright screen colour with its printed version

## Understand it

- **Schemes**: pick one main colour, one accent, and neutrals (black, grey, white). Complementary colours (opposite on the wheel) give energy; analogous colours (neighbours) feel calm.
- **Contrast**: text must stand out from its background. The standard used on the web is at least **4.5:1** for body text. Light yellow text on white fails; dark navy on white passes easily. Check with a contrast checker.
- **Screen vs print**: screens mix **light** in **RGB** (red, green, blue); printers mix **ink** in **CMYK** (cyan, magenta, yellow, black). Some bright screen colours cannot be printed — they come out duller. For print, design in CMYK or ask the printer for a proof.

Colour also carries meaning: never let colour be the ONLY way you show something (some people are colour-blind).

![Light versus ink](media:core/rgb-cmyk.svg)

## Key words

- **RGB:** red, green, blue light — screens
- **CMYK:** cyan, magenta, yellow, black ink — print
- **Contrast ratio:** how much text stands out from its background

## Read and watch

- [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — Type two colours and see if text on them can be read (aim for 4.5:1).
- [Adobe Color wheel](https://color.adobe.com/create/color-wheel) — Build a colour scheme from the colour wheel.

## Practise at home

- Check the contrast of three signs or flyers you see
- Find one that fails and suggest a fix

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Start with navy text on white and one bright accent; check it, then vary.
- **If you already can:** Design the same flyer in a complementary and an analogous scheme and test both for contrast.

## Assessed this week

- Why might a bright green on your screen print dull?

lessons.title: Images: resolution, cropping and rights
lessons.summary: A picture must be sharp enough to print, cropped with purpose, and yours to use.
objectives: Explain 72 vs 300 ppi
Crop an image to strengthen it
Use images legally and credit them
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Print the same photo at two resolutions
- Crop one photo three ways and pick the strongest
- Find a free-to-use image and write its credit

## Understand it

- **Resolution**: an image is made of pixels. Screens need about 72–150 pixels per inch; **print needs about 300**. A small image from a website looks fine on screen and blurry on paper. Never stretch an image bigger than it is.
- **Cropping** removes what does not help: cut to the subject, keep eyes on the upper third, leave room in the direction a person is looking.
- **Rights**: an image online is NOT free to use. Use your own photos, images with a licence that allows it (Creative Commons, Unsplash), and **credit** them. Ask permission before using a photo of a person — especially a child.
- **Alt text**: on screen, describe the image for people who cannot see it.
- **AI-made images**: if you generate a picture with an AI tool, check the tool's terms allow your use, say it was AI-made in the credit, look closely for errors (hands, text, signs), and never make a fake photo of a real person.

![72 versus 300 ppi](media:core/resolution.svg)

## Key words

- **Resolution:** how many pixels per inch
- **Crop:** cut away part of an image
- **Licence:** the rules for using someone else's work
- **Alt text:** a description of an image for people who cannot see it

## Read and watch

- [Creative Commons licences](https://creativecommons.org/about/cclicenses/) — What you may and may not do with an image someone else made.
- [Unsplash licence](https://unsplash.com/license) — Free photos, and the rules for using them.

## Practise at home

- Take three photos of one object and crop each differently
- Find an image with a Creative Commons licence and write its credit

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Use the crop tool's rule-of-thirds grid.
- **If you already can:** Work out the largest size, in cm, a 1200 × 900 pixel photo can be printed at 300 ppi.

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Read the brief and list what must be on the flyer
- Sketch three thumbnails, choose one

## Understand it

A **brief** says who it is for, what it must say, the size, and the deadline. Designers start with **thumbnails** — tiny quick sketches — before the computer. If you ask an AI tool for headline ideas, treat them as a first draft: check each one against the brief, change what does not fit, and note what you changed.

Your flyer needs: a headline, the key facts (what, when, where, cost), a short body, one strong image, and a call to action ("Register at …").

Before printing, run the **proof checklist**:

1. Spelling, dates and times checked by someone else.
2. Hierarchy: the three-second test.
3. Everything aligned to a grid.
4. Text contrast at least 4.5:1.
5. Images sharp at print size, and allowed.
6. Nothing important within 3 mm of the edge.

lessons.title: Folded work and print preparation: bleed, trim and safe area
lessons.summary: Printers cut paper, and the cut is never perfect. Bleed, trim and the safe area protect your design.
objectives: Explain bleed, trim and safe area

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Mark bleed, trim and safe area on a printed page
- Set up a tri-fold with bleed in Canva or Scribus
- Fold a paper mock-up to check the panel order

## Understand it

A print shop prints on bigger paper and **cuts** it down — and the blade can move a millimetre or two.

- **Trim**: where the paper is meant to be cut (the finished size).
- **Bleed**: extend background colours and photos **3 mm beyond the trim**, so a slightly-off cut never leaves a white edge.
- **Safe area**: keep text and logos at least **3–5 mm inside the trim**, so nothing important is cut off.

In Canva: **File → Show print bleed**; in Scribus: set bleed in **Document setup**.

A **tri-fold brochure** is one sheet folded into six panels. The front cover is on the outside right; the inside panels read left to right. Always make a **paper mock-up** before printing.

![Bleed, trim and safe area](media:core/page-anatomy.svg)

![Tri-fold panel order](media:core/trifold.svg)

## Key words

- **Bleed:** colour extended 3 mm past the trim
- **Trim:** the finished size where paper is cut
- **Safe area:** the zone that keeps text away from the cut

## Read and watch

- [Scribus](https://www.scribus.net/) — Free, professional desktop publishing for Windows, Mac and Linux — what the print trade uses for free.

- Find a printed item with a white edge where the cut went wrong

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Fold the mock-up first; number every panel before designing.

## What to do

- Export your flyer as PDF (print) with bleed
- Pre-flight it: fonts, images, bleed, spelling
- Write a print brief: size, quantity, paper, deadline, contact

## Understand it

Send printers a **PDF**, never a Word or Canva link: a PDF keeps your fonts, layout and images exactly.

- Canva: **Share → Download → PDF Print**, tick **Crop marks and bleed**.
- Scribus/LibreOffice: **Export as PDF**, with bleed and high-quality images.

**Pre-flight** before sending: fonts embedded, images 300 ppi at print size, bleed present, colours checked, and the text proofread by someone else. Name the file clearly: `2026-03-14_Showcase-Flyer_A5_v3.pdf`.

A **print brief** tells the print shop: size and orientation, quantity, paper (weight in gsm, matte or gloss), single- or double-sided, finishing (folding, cutting), deadline, budget, and your phone number. Ask for a **proof** before the full run.

![The export window for a print PDF: bleed, crop marks, embedded fonts, full-resolution images](media:core/shots/dtp-pdf-export.png)

## Key words

- **PDF:** a file format that keeps a layout exactly
- **Pre-flight:** the final technical check before printing
- **GSM:** paper weight in grams per square metre

## Read and watch

- [GCFGlobal — Beginning Graphic Design](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/beginning-graphic-design/) — Free, short, illustrated lessons on layout, type and colour; no account needed.

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Plan the four pages as a flat plan
- Write, photograph and design your pages
- Pre-flight, export and present to the panel

## Understand it

Your magazine is the term's work in one publication. You need:

- a **flat plan**: a small drawing of all four pages showing what goes where;
- a **cover** with masthead, a strong image and two cover lines;
- **three inside pages** on one grid, with consistent styles, at least one story, one photo story and one data graphic (link to Data Appreciation!);
- **legal images**, credited, with consent for people;
- a **print-ready PDF** with bleed;
- a **three-minute presentation**: your choices and why.

Go back to your earlier work before you start: the week 4 hierarchy, the week 5 grid and the week 10 bleed set-up are what this magazine is built from, so use them again.

The panel will ask about YOUR decisions — the grid, the hierarchy, the colours. That is how they know the work is yours.

![Plan every page on the grid](media:core/grid.svg)

## Key words

- **Flat plan:** a map of every page of a publication
- **Cover line:** a short teaser for a story inside

## Read and watch

- [Scribus](https://www.scribus.net/) — Free, professional desktop publishing for Windows, Mac and Linux — what the print trade uses for free.
- [GCFGlobal — Beginning Graphic Design](https://edu.gcfglobal.org/en/beginning-graphic-design/) — Free, short, illustrated lessons on layout, type and colour; no account needed.
- [WebAIM Contrast Checker](https://webaim.org/resources/contrastchecker/) — Type two colours and see if text on them can be read (aim for 4.5:1).

## Practise at home

- Rehearse your three-minute presentation
- Get one person to proofread every page

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Use a Canva magazine template as the starting grid; replace every element.
- **If you already can:** Produce a printed copy and a screen version with alt text for every image.

## Assessed this week

- Your four-page magazine: upload the print-ready PDF and your flat plan, and describe your design decisions.
- Name one design decision you made and why it helps the reader.

You may be asked to explain your work: the marks are for your own thinking.
